desired_state_summary: The GDD requires a Windows Standalone build as part of the Required Scope (Section 3) and Technical Strategy (Section 5), with the canonical gameplay scene registered in Unity Build Settings before that delivery obligation can be considered complete. The GDD also defines an extensive set of required development-process invariants governing the AI-assisted pipeline: minimal-context dispatch, isolated-branch/workspace execution with no concurrent edits to the same Unity assets, a scene-builder exclusive-write lock for `DoorPrototypeSceneBuilder.cs`/`DoorPrototype.unity`, compile-before-validation, failed-task scope-reduction retry policy, a planning token-budget ceiling, mandatory human inspection/merge/playtesting authority, agent scope/canon discipline, preservation of non-canonical stub scenes as a human decision, a boundary on what generated development-time art import does and does not imply, credential handling outside source control, and a runtime prohibition on generative AI in the shipped game. Section 3's Player Experience Success Criteria are required validation obligations that must be attached to the concrete work items (owned by other domain workers) that actually implement the underlying behavior, not treated as separate gameplay features. Stretch goals and explicitly excluded systems must be enumerated and kept out of required Milestone 1 work.

validation_requirements.requirement: A first-time player understands that clicking a door sends the wizard to it, and that reaching the door is not enough — the automatic opening timer still requires five safe, uninterrupted seconds.

Door interaction requires accurate cursor target selection only on the initial click; the wizard's automatic approach, the timer's automatic start on arrival, and tolerance of normal cursor drift after selection are all readable to a first-time player.

requirement_overlays.reason: GDD Section 4 states Player Experience Success Criteria are required validation obligations that must be attached to the work item(s) that already own the underlying behavior rather than becoming separate gameplay features. door-open-interaction (doors domain) owns click-to-approach selection, arrival detection, and the automatic five-second opening timer described by these criteria.

validation_requirements.requirement: Crossing an opened doorway causes automatic close-and-lock with no second player input required, and this behavior is readable/expected by a first-time player.
Failure caused by waiting too long — allowing a locked door to break under sustained pursuer pressure — is readable to the player through durability/breach feedback.

requirement_overlays.reason: The remainder of the door-interaction Player Experience Success Criterion concerns automatic close-and-lock behavior and breach-caused failure readability, both owned by the door lifecycle/durability implementation rather than door opening/selection.

validation_requirements.requirement: The player understands that enemies left alive remain a threat: leaving them alive means locking a door while they attack it, and later encountering them if that door breaks through.

requirement_overlays.reason: This Player Experience Success Criterion describes the perceivability of the locked-door attack/persistent-pursuer consequence, which is owned by the locked-door enemy attack behavior (enemy_behavior domain) rather than by door durability state itself.

validation_requirements.requirement: Encounters use three to eight enemies and never exceed fifteen active enemies at once.

requirement_overlays.reason: The encounter-size and active-enemy-cap success criterion is a validation obligation on the runtime foundation that enforces the fifteen-active-enemy ceiling and admission policy, not a new gameplay feature.

validation_requirements.requirement: Failure caused by poor positioning is readable to the player through health/damage feedback, as part of the required 'failure is readable' success criterion.

requirement_overlays.reason: Section 4 explicitly requires Player Experience Success Criteria to be represented as validation requirements on the owning work; poor-positioning failure readability is expressed primarily through the Player Health system's continuous health feedback.

validation_requirements.requirement: Failure caused by low mana is readable to the player through the mana indicator, as part of the required 'failure is readable' success criterion.

requirement_overlays.reason: The low-mana portion of the failure-readability success criterion is owned by the Player Mana system's continuous mana feedback.

validation_requirements.requirement: Failure caused by using Force Wave without an immediate threat and then lacking it during a later critical moment, due to its long cooldown, is readable to the player.

requirement_overlays.reason: The Force Wave misuse/unavailability portion of the failure-readability success criterion is owned by the Force Wave spell's cooldown/feedback behavior.

non_code_requirements.title: No concurrent Unity asset edits

gdd_evidence.reference: Section 4 - Agent-Assisted Development Workflow
gdd_evidence.requirement: Tasks that depend on unfinished work, or that require changes to the same scripts, scenes, or prefabs, are completed sequentially. Agents do not modify the same Unity assets concurrently.

gdd_evidence.requirement: Agents cannot add mechanics, redesign the game, or expand the scope without developer approval.

gdd_evidence.reference: Section 5 - Technical Strategy
gdd_evidence.requirement: The finished Windows game will not use generative AI at runtime; enemy behavior, spell effects, doors, damage, and pursuit run locally through standard Unity systems. The game requires no external AI service, API key, token usage, or network connection after it is built.

gdd_evidence.requirement: 'Generative AI during play' is explicitly excluded scope.

non_code_requirements.evidence: Directly and explicitly required/excluded scope in the current GDD; a non-code technical constraint on the shipped game rather than a build step or agent-process rule.

gdd_evidence.reference: Section 5 - Runtime Implementation
gdd_evidence.requirement: Development-time art acquisition may use approved tools that can generate isometric tiles, props, and directional sprites. Those outputs are imported into Unity as normal assets; they do not imply automatic prefab creation, collision setup, sorting configuration, or gameplay integration.

non_code_requirements.evidence: Directly stated in Section 5 Runtime Implementation and reiterated in the Technical Strategy generative-tools note; a required process/validation constraint on content/asset pipeline work rather than gameplay implementation.

gdd_evidence.requirement: The presence of the non-canonical Assets/Scenes stub scenes is repository evidence, not a design requirement; their deletion, retention, or repurposing is a human decision, and agents/reconciliation steps must not delete or reinterpret them merely to make scene inventory evidence cleaner.

non_code_requirements.evidence: Directly stated in Section 5 Current Prototype Scene Evidence; confirmed present via Assets/Scenes/DoorPrototype.unity and Assets/Scenes/SampleScene.unity glob results.

gdd_evidence.reference: Section 4 - Shared Context and Coordination Rules
gdd_evidence.requirement: Scene-authoring work that changes objects generated or maintained through Assets/NoSafeCircle/DoorPrototype/Editor/DoorPrototypeSceneBuilder.cs must take exclusive-write locks on both that builder and Assets/NoSafeCircle/DoorPrototype/Scenes/DoorPrototype.unity.

non_code_requirements.evidence: Directly stated as a required durable process rule in Section 4; per-task applications are represented as matching exclusive_resources entries across domain workers whose implementation writes through the builder/scene.

non_code_requirements.title: Development Agent Ownership Invariants

gdd_evidence.reference: Section 4 - Development Agent Ownership Invariants
gdd_evidence.requirement: The listed ownership boundaries are required development-process constraints that must be preserved by planning, reconciliation, implementation, and validation agents. An agent must not bypass another agent's owned runtime interface merely because both systems interact; shared-write conflicts are sequencing/locking concerns, not proof of a dependency unless one task actually requires behavior another task must create first.

non_code_requirements.evidence: Directly stated as a required cross-cutting process constraint in Section 4; the specific per-agent ownership boundaries (Wizard Combat, Enemy Pursuit, Door and Interaction, victory coordination, Dungeon Encounter, Unity Validation) are represented as acceptance criteria/dependencies on their respective owning work items across the other domain workers.
